A close reading for the week

“buy the flowers herself”

Mrs Dalloway · the opening

A woman decides to fetch her own flowers for a party. Within a few sentences the errand has taken her back thirty years, to a house in the country and the man she did not marry.

Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.1

For Lucy had her work cut out for her. The doors would be taken off their hinges;2 Rumpelmayer’s men were coming. And then, thought Clarissa Dalloway, what a morning—fresh as if issued to children on a beach.

  1. 1

    The first sentence

    The first sentence is domestic, ordinary and a little strange. Mrs Dalloway “said she would buy the flowers herself”: reported speech, mid-conversation, with a whole household implied (the servants who might have gone instead). Woolf drops us into a life already in motion, seen from a slight, sidelong angle. The famous novel of consciousness begins with an errand, because Woolf believed a life is fully present in its smallest choices.

  2. 2

    Doors off their hinges

    The detail is practical (the doors will come off their hinges for the caterers), and it also looks ahead. All day the novel will take things off their hinges: memory swinging open into the present, the boundary between minds giving way. The image also prepares for the hinge that squeaks a few lines later, the sound that takes Clarissa thirty years back.
